title: There are people who can celebrate you while you are beneath them.
paragraphs: There are people who can celebrate you while you are beneath them.
But the moment God begins lifting you higher than their comfort level, their love changes into suspicion, then fear, then hatred.
That was Saul.
And if you only read the story casually, you might think Saul was simply jealous. But the deeper Hebrew context reveals something far more terrifying:
Saul was a man who lost intimacy with God long before he lost the throne.
David’s success merely exposed what was already dead inside Saul.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
The turning point begins in 1 Samuel chapter 15 when Saul disobeys God regarding Amalek.
Most modern readers miss the weight of the Hebrew wording.
God commanded Saul to devote Amalek to destruction using the Hebrew word:
חֵרֶם (ḥerem)
This does not merely mean “destroy.”
It means something placed fully under God’s judgment — irrevocably surrendered to divine justice.
Saul partially obeyed.
And partial obedience in Scripture is rebellion wearing religious clothing.
The prophet Samuel tells Saul:

“For rebellion is as the sin of divination…”
— 1 Samuel 15:23
The Hebrew word for rebellion is:
מֶרִי (meri)
It implies stubborn resistance against rightful authority.
Saul was not confused.
God saw it.
He knew.
And from that moment, something catastrophic happened spiritually.
1 Samuel 16:14 says:
“But the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul…”
The Hebrew reads:

וְרוּחַ יְהוָה סָרָה מֵעִם שָׁאוּל
Ve-ruach YHWH sarah me’im Sha’ul
The word סָרָה (sarah) means “turned away,” “departed,” or “removed itself.”
This was not emotional sadness.
This was divine withdrawal.
And here is what most people don’t realize…
When the presence of God leaves a man, insecurity rushes in to fill the empty throne inside his heart.
Saul still had a crown.
Still had an army.
Still sat on a throne.
But heaven had already rejected him.
And deep down…
he knew it.
Then David appears.
A shepherd boy carrying oil on his head and worship in his spirit.
David enters Saul’s life first as a servant.
He plays the harp to calm Saul’s torment.
Imagine the tragedy.
The man Saul would later try to murder was the same man once sent by God to soothe him.
That is what unchecked pride does.
It attacks the very people sent to help heal you.
When David kills Goliath, Israel erupts in celebration.
The women sing:

“Saul has slain his thousands,
and David his ten thousands.”
— 1 Samuel 18:7
Now look carefully at Saul’s response.
The Hebrew says:

וַיִּחַר לְשָׁאוּל מְאֹד
Vayichar leSha’ul me’od
Literally:
“Saul burned greatly.”
This is not mild jealousy.
The Hebrew imagery is combustion.
Internal fire.
Consuming rage.
Then verse 9 says:
“And Saul eyed David from that day forward.”
The Hebrew word is:
עָוַן (‘avan) in related conceptual framing of twisted perception and hostile scrutiny, though the direct verb used conveys watching with suspicion and hostility.
Saul became obsessed with David.
Why?
Because David represented everything Saul used to be before pride corrupted him.
David had intimacy with God.
Courage.
Purity of worship.
Dependence on the Lord.
Saul no longer possessed those things.
And instead of repenting…
he competed.
That is the danger of a heart separated from God.
You stop being inspired by grace and become threatened by it.
David’s success exposed Saul’s insecurity.
Notice this carefully:
David never tried to steal Saul’s throne.
Saul lost peace fighting an enemy that God never told him to fight.
Some people destroy themselves battling imaginary rivals because they cannot accept God’s sovereignty.
Saul heard prophecy that the kingdom would leave him, but instead of humbling himself, he clung harder to power.
That spirit still exists today.
People who cannot celebrate another person’s blessing usually fear losing their own identity.
But identity rooted in God does not panic when someone else rises.
Only insecure flesh does that.
There is another layer hidden in the text.
1 Samuel repeatedly says:
“The LORD was with David.”
In Hebrew:
יְהוָה עִמּוֹ (YHWH ‘immo)
“The LORD with him.”
This phrase appears again and again because the true issue was never military success.
It was presence.
Saul recognized God’s favor had shifted.
And instead of seeking restoration…
he sought elimination.
Read that again.
Some people would rather destroy what convicts them than repent before God.
Saul’s hatred intensified because David succeeded without striving in the flesh.
David trusted God.
Saul manipulated circumstances.
David worshiped.
Saul performed.
David repented quickly when confronted.
Saul protected his image.
That is why David could recover after sin while Saul collapsed under his own corruption.
Brokenness before God always has more hope than pride before men.
One of the saddest verses in the entire story comes later.
Saul seeks guidance from a medium at Endor.
The king once chosen by God now seeks forbidden spiritual counsel because heaven has gone silent to him.
The Hebrew term for medium is:
בַּעֲלַת־אוֹב (ba‘alat-ov)
A “mistress of spirits” or necromancer.
Saul became the very thing he was commanded to oppose.
Sin never stays contained.
What you refuse to kill spiritually will eventually rule you.
Meanwhile David, though imperfect, continually returned to God in repentance.
That is the real difference between Saul and David.
Not perfection versus failure.
But pride versus repentance.
Saul wanted the throne more than God.
David wanted God even when he lost everything else.
And heaven responds differently to those two hearts.
But this story is not merely ancient history.
It is a mirror.
Some people reading this are exhausted because you are living like Saul.
Comparing.
Watching others obsessively.
Secretly angry when someone else succeeds.
Terrified of becoming irrelevant.
God saw it.
You knew.
And the deeper issue may not be jealousy itself.
It may be distance from God.
Because when intimacy with God fades, human approval becomes oxygen.
Then another person’s success feels like your death.
But the Gospel destroys that slavery.
Jesus Christ succeeded where Saul failed.
Unlike Saul, Jesus did not cling to power selfishly.
Philippians 2:6-8 says Christ “emptied Himself.”
The Greek phrase is:
ἐκένωσεν ἑαυτόν (ekenōsen heauton)
“He emptied Himself.”
King Jesus laid down glory willingly to save sinners.
Saul grasped for a throne and lost everything.
Jesus surrendered His throne temporarily and gained an eternal Kingdom.
That contrast changes everything.
And through the cross, Christ offers a new heart.
Not one ruled by insecurity.
Not one poisoned by comparison.
Not one burning every time God blesses someone else.
But a heart secure in the Father.
A heart that can celebrate others because identity is anchored in grace, not status.
That kind of freedom only comes through repentance and surrender to Jesus Christ.
Not self-improvement.
Not religious performance.
Transformation.
Some of you need to stop chasing Saul’s crown and start seeking David’s heart.
Because the throne without God becomes torment.
But even a wilderness with God becomes peace.
And maybe that conviction you feel right now is not condemnation.
Maybe it is mercy.
The same God who rejected Saul’s rebellion still welcomed David’s repentance.
That door is still open through Jesus Christ.
But it will not stay open forever.
